nm_rabbit_ears_slabs.blurb: Rabbit Ears Slabs lies in the western Organ Mountains near Las Cruces, in the canyon below the Rabbit Ears. The climbing is slabby, one to three pitches long, and nearly all of it is protected with traditional gear; there is one bolted line and one aid route. Grades are friendly: the bulk of the sixteen climbs sit at 5.7 or 5.8, with a few easier ones, a handful at 5.10 and a single 5.11. Gullies split the base into two main slab sections, and higher up the rock breaks into scrambling. Expect a short, thorny bushwhack to reach the foot of the walls. A good stop for moderate multi-pitch practice.

nm_lambda.blurb: Lambda is a formation in the North Organs, near Las Cruces, facing The Citadel across the canyon. Every route is traditional, and most are multi-pitch lines of two to five pitches on the south, west and north sides. Difficulty is moderate: a dozen of the sixteen climbs are 5.7 or 5.8, backed by two at 5.9 and two at 5.10. It is a committed day, since the cairned approach trail takes roughly one to two hours depending on how far you can drive. The way down is a gully on the south side, using rappel stations. A standard Organ trad rack handles it, and this is a quiet, off-the-beaten-path objective.

nm_checkerboard_wall.blurb: Checkerboard Wall is the main attraction of the Dona Ana Mountains north of Las Cruces: a large east-facing cliff more than 500 feet tall and nearly twice as wide, cut by crack systems that give it a patchwork look. Routes run up to five pitches and are mostly traditional, with a few bolted lines mixed in. Grades are approachable, clustering between 5.7 and 5.9 with a couple at 5.10 and one easier warm-up line. Getting here involves a rough desert dirt road where some clearance helps, then roughly half an hour on a well-worn trail. Rappelling is the usual way down; the long south-end walk-off is rarely used.

nm_crack_house_aka_estante_edge_the.blurb: The Crack House, also called Estante Edge, is a short south-facing basalt cliff along the canyon rim at White Rock, near Los Alamos. It is a wall for crack climbers: about sixteen lines, ten of them top-rope and six traditional leads. Nearly everything is 5.11, with five at 5.12 and a lone 5.10. The routes are brief, around 45 feet, and follow crack systems with only a few face lines, giving White Rock its densest collection of hard cracks. You reach the base by scrambling down a gully from the rim and walking along the foot of the cliff. Bring a rack and slings for anchors.

nm_45_boulder.blurb: The 45 Degree Boulder is a compact sub-area of the Dungeon, a steep rhyolite sport venue above Los Alamos, tucked just right of the Main Wall. Its sixteen routes are almost all bolted, compact and overhanging, with quality that varies from line to line. This is terrain for strong climbers: nine routes are 5.12, a few more reach 5.13 and 5.14, and only a handful are 5.10 or 5.11, so there is little here for beginners. The Dungeon as a whole is treated as a summer crag, sitting at close to 8,000 feet where it stays cooler than lower valley areas. Reach it by following the trail to the Main Wall and continuing right.

nm_bush_shark_area.blurb: The Bush Shark Area is a cluster of mostly traditional routes in Echo Canyon on the west side of the Sandia Mountains, close to the crest and reached by one of the shortest approaches in the range. A rare spire summit gives the area its name, and nearby walls hold lines of two to four pitches. Grades start at 5.9, where the largest group sits, continue through 5.10 and 5.11, and top out with a few 5.12s and a single 5.13. A standard Sandia rack with doubles in the small and medium cam sizes works well. Descents are by rappel, and a pair of ropes or a 70 m rope makes them straightforward.

nm_sunny_side_right_end.blurb: Sunny Side (Right End) is the right-hand half of a long limestone cliff at the Tunnel, a roadside sport crag east of Alamogordo. This end is regarded as the best stone on the cliff. Climbing is mostly gently overhanging: crimpy starts, a vertical middle section with big holds, and a slabby top with slopers. The grades are stiff, with nearly all sixteen routes falling between 5.11 and 5.13 and 5.12 making up the bulk; there is one easy outlier at 5.7. Shade is limited, from about an hour to half a day depending on the season, and less near the winter solstice. Traffic is light, though road noise and graffiti at the base are drawbacks.

nm_upper_park.blurb: Some eight miles northeast of Monticello, Upper Park is a handful of volcanic cliffs a short way up the road past the Luna Park campground. Its sixteen climbs mix sport, traditional and top-rope lines, mostly moderate: eight sit at 5.8, a few at 5.9 and 5.10, with a pair at 5.7 and one at 5.6. The walk is only a few minutes, up the road and then down a climber's trail to the taller cliffs. Trees shade the belays and the ground is flat, which suits casual days. Rock on this upper tier can be loose in places, so test holds before trusting them.
